fixes.explanation: That's the word. Verse 1 says, "…he who hates correction is stupid." It's blunt, and it sits right next to the person who loves discipline and so loves knowledge. Nobody enjoys hearing the timer was set wrong, but I'd rather hear it before the batch comes out burnt.

A shield is a strong picture, and I can see why it came to mind, friend. But verse 4 says a wife of noble character is "…her husband’s crown…" A crown sits on the head where everybody can see it. The other side of the verse is the wife who causes shame, who is "…like decay in his bones."
Shame shows up in verse 4, with the wife who causes it. Verse 6 is about words, though. The words of the wicked "lie in wait for blood," but the speech of the upright "rescues them."

I think the first half pulled you along, and I don't blame you. The wicked are overthrown and perish, yes. But the verse turns right there: "…but the house of the righteous will stand." It sets the wicked on one side and the house of the righteous on the other.

Family matters a lot, and verse 4 even talks about a husband and wife. But verse 8 says a man is praised "…according to his wisdom…" Wisdom is the measure here, and the other side of the verse says "…a twisted mind is despised."

Land does come up soon, in verse 11: "The one who works his land will have plenty of food…" In verse 9, though, the self-important man lacks something else. The verse says he lacks "food." Hold onto that land for verse 11.

That's it. Verse 14 says, "By fruitful speech a man is filled with good things, and the work of his hands returns to him." Both halves of the verse are about what a man does, with his mouth and with his hands. The word that fills in the blank is speech.

Handing an insult right back is easy, and I get why you picked it. But verse 16 doesn't say that. It says, "A fool’s anger is known at once…" and then it turns to the prudent man, who "…overlooks an insult."

Riches would be a nice reward, but verse 18 doesn't promise them. It sets two tongues side by side. Speaking rashly is "like a piercing sword," and the tongue of the wise "brings healing." The sword hurts and the healing mends, friend.

Power might sound like what counselors want. But verse 20 sets two kinds of hearts side by side. Deceit is in the hearts of those who devise evil, but the counselors of peace "have joy." Joy is the word, friend, not power.

Boldness can be a good thing, but verse 22 doesn't name it. The verse sets lying lips, which are "detestable to the LORD," next to "…those who deal faithfully are His delight." The word is faithfully, friend, and it stands opposite lying.

Right. Verse 25 says, "Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up." A good word is what lifts the heart that anxiety weighs down. I've seen a kind word do more for a worn-out stamper than a whole box of fresh dough.
